teen-weekend-anchor.say: On the weekend, an hour or two later than usual is the limit. Sleeping until noon on Saturday shoves the body clock back again, and Monday morning gets that much worse.

teen-morning-light.label: Light first thing
teen-morning-light.say: First thing after waking — open the curtains, get outside for a few minutes. Light is the strongest tool there is for pulling a body clock earlier, and it beats ten more minutes in bed.

teen-screen-limit.label: The phone's bedtime
teen-screen-limit.say: The real damage from screens isn't blue light — it's that one more video eats the hour they should have been asleep. Rather than banning the phone, agree together on a time when the phone goes to bed too, and have it charge outside the bedroom. At this age, agreed beats imposed.

teen-no-blame-talk.label: Ask, don't scold
teen-no-blame-talk.say: At this age, the more you scold the less truth you get. Try asking instead: 'Do you feel like you're getting enough? Is the morning rough?' Getting him to say it himself does more than ten sentences from you.

teen-refer.label: When it needs help beyond the house
teen-refer.say: If he's so tired he's sleeping through class, or the mood is clearly low and he doesn't want to go to school, that's worth a doctor — start with the pediatrician, or a child and adolescent mental health specialist. **And if he ever says anything about not wanting to be alive, or that there's no point to any of it — that doesn't wait. Call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. It's free, and it's answered around the clock.**

stress-name-it.label: Say it out loud first
stress-name-it.say: Just saying 'I'm under a lot right now' out loud, to someone who's actually listening, takes some of the tension out of the body. If you want to talk, I'm here for it.

stress-micro-break.label: Fifteen minutes that belong to you
stress-micro-break.say: Fifteen minutes a day that belong to you — no messages, nothing for anyone else, one small thing you actually want to do. It doesn't have to be long. It does have to be every day.

stress-caregiver-respite.label: Respite isn't a luxury
stress-caregiver-respite.say: Respite care was built for exactly this, and using it isn't slacking off. If you go down there's nobody holding the house up — looking after yourself is part of looking after him. **The Eldercare Locator, 1-800-677-1116 on weekdays, will connect you to whatever's available where you live.**

stress-breathing.label: Breathe out longer than you breathe in
stress-breathing.say: When you feel like you're about to go under: breathe in for four, out for six, ten times over. Making the out-breath longer than the in-breath is what tells the body it's allowed to let go.

stress-move.label: Moving beats collapsing
stress-move.say: When the stress is high the body actually wants to move — a brisk twenty-minute walk shakes it off better than sinking into the couch with your phone.

stress-refer.label: When it's time for a professional
stress-refer.say: If this has run two weeks or more, and even the things you used to enjoy do nothing for you — that isn't you being weak, it's the point where talking to a professional is the right move. Your primary care doctor is a perfectly good place to start. **And if you're having thoughts of not wanting to be alive, that doesn't wait: call or text 988, any hour, and someone will answer.**

meno-normalize.label: This is not a failing
meno-normalize.say: Menopause isn't an illness — it's your hormones recalibrating. The hot flashes, the rough sleep, the mood swings are real physical responses. You're not imagining it, and you're not being weak.

meno-layers.label: Layers, a little fan, a cooler room
meno-layers.say: For hot flashes, the unglamorous stuff works best: a cardigan you can peel off, a little fan in your purse, and a bedroom cooled down before you turn in. Simple, but it's what actually brings relief fastest.

meno-triggers.label: Find your own trigger list
meno-triggers.say: Spicy food, hot drinks, alcohol, coffee, stress — everyone's triggers are different. Jot down what came right before a hot flash for a few days. Once you spot your pattern, it's much easier to dodge.

meno-exercise.label: Regular exercise
meno-exercise.say: Regular exercise has solid evidence for menopause sleep and mood — and it protects your bones and heart at the same time, right when bone loss speeds up. Two birds, one stone.

meno-sleep-link.label: Two different sleep problems
meno-sleep-link.say: People assume menopause simply equals bad sleep — but waking up drenched at 3 a.m. and being a light sleeper in general are two different problems, and they're tackled separately. You don't have to accept the whole package as your fate.

meno-food.label: Plant estrogens from food
meno-food.say: Soy milk, tofu, edamame — soy foods naturally contain isoflavones, and the amounts you get from a normal diet are quite safe. Start with the grocery aisle before you reach for bottles.

meno-isoflavone.label: Soy isoflavone supplements
meno-isoflavone.dailyCap: Follow the product label, and don't stack it with other isoflavone products
meno-isoflavone.say: Soy isoflavone supplements have middling-to-weak evidence for hot flashes — some women notice a difference, some don't. Worth a try if you're curious, but don't expect a miracle pill. **The part that matters most: if you've had breast cancer or any hormone-related cancer, or you're on anti-hormone medication like tamoxifen, do not take these without asking your doctor** — that's not a decision to make alone.

meno-hrt-blocked.label: Hormone therapy
meno-hrt-blocked.say: Hormone therapy is a prescription decision — whether it's right for you and for how long depends on your personal history, and that's for your gynecologist or primary care doctor to weigh with you. I won't recommend it — but I will say this: if symptoms are wrecking your daily life, asking about it is a perfectly legitimate road. You don't have to just endure.

meno-refer.label: When to see a doctor
meno-refer.say: **Bleeding again after your periods have fully stopped — don't sit on that one; see a gynecologist promptly.** And if low mood has lasted more than two weeks, or symptoms are bad enough to derail work and daily life, that's not something to white-knuckle through — it's worth a doctor's visit.

period-heat.label: Heat on the lower belly
period-heat.say: A heating pad or a hot water bottle on the lower belly is one of the few things here with real research behind it — and you can do it tonight. A warm bath counts too.

period-movement.label: Gentle movement beats lying still
period-movement.say: When it hurts, all you want is to lie down — but a gentle walk or some easy stretching gets the blood moving and usually hurts less than staying curled up all day. Nobody's telling you to go work out; just don't stay balled up for two days.

period-track.label: Keep track of your own pattern
period-track.say: Write down when it starts, how many days it hurts, and how bad. Knowing your own pattern means you stop getting ambushed by it — and it's the single most useful thing you can hand a doctor.

period-pms-plan.label: Plan the days before
period-pms-plan.say: If you get irritable, puffy and weepy in the days before — that isn't a bad temperament. Once you know roughly which days they are, you can move the hard meetings and the big conversations off them.

period-food.label: Eating through those days
period-food.say: In the days before, less salt and less caffeine means less bloating and tenderness. During, you're losing iron — leafy greens, red meat and beans are worth leaning on.

period-tcm.label: Acupuncture and herbal routes
period-tcm.say: If you lean toward acupuncture or Chinese herbal medicine for this, that's a legitimate road — look for a licensed practitioner, and most states license acupuncturists. The one thing not to do is order a formula off the internet: the classic 'women's' blends aren't right for everyone, and they aren't meant for every point in your cycle. **And tell your regular doctor and your pharmacist what you're taking — herbs and prescriptions can genuinely clash.**

period-painkiller-blocked.label: Which painkiller, and how much
period-painkiller-blocked.say: Which painkiller and how to take it is a question for your doctor or pharmacist, not for me. But one thing I do want to say plainly: **taking something for period pain is not a failure of willpower.** If it's interfering with your life, it deserves to be dealt with.

period-refer.label: When to see a gynecologist
period-refer.say: **Pain bad enough to miss work or school, pain that makes you throw up or pass out, or bleeding that suddenly gets much heavier — see a gynecologist. Don't tough it out.** Endometriosis routinely goes undiagnosed for years, and the main reason is that everybody assumes periods are supposed to hurt. Bleeding between periods, or missing one for over a month when pregnancy isn't the answer, is also worth an appointment.

iron-test-first.label: Get the blood test before you supplement
iron-test-first.say: Being worn out, dizzy and pale doesn't automatically mean low iron — get the blood work first and look at hemoglobin and ferritin. Supplementing only helps if that's actually what's wrong, and **too much iron does real harm**, so guessing your way through this one isn't a good plan.

iron-food.label: Iron from food
iron-food.say: Red meat, liver, clams and oysters, beans, and dark leafy greens. Iron from animal foods absorbs far better than iron from plants, so if you eat vegetarian you have to be more deliberate about it.

iron-vitc.label: Pair it with vitamin C
iron-vitc.say: A genuinely useful trick: have something with vitamin C alongside the iron food — oranges, strawberries, bell peppers, tomatoes. It makes a real difference to how much you actually absorb.

iron-avoid-tea.label: Not with tea or coffee
iron-avoid-tea.say: The tannins in tea and coffee block iron from being absorbed. Wait an hour or two after the meal before you have them — costs nothing, and it matters.

iron-supplement.label: Iron supplements
iron-supplement.dailyCap: Dose and duration go by your doctor's or pharmacist's instructions — never increase it on your own
iron-supplement.say: If the blood work does show you're low, iron is one of the few things on any of these lists where the right supplement genuinely makes you feel different. But **the dose and how long to take it are the doctor's to set**, and the cause has to be found first — unexplained iron deficiency in an adult is sometimes slow bleeding somewhere in the gut. Fair warning: iron very commonly causes constipation and an unhappy stomach, and it has to be spaced apart from thyroid medicine and certain antibiotics.

iron-cause-blocked.label: Why you're low
iron-cause-blocked.say: Why you're low on iron isn't mine to judge — heavy periods, bleeding in the digestive tract, trouble absorbing it, all possible. That's what the doctor works out.

iron-refer.label: When the cause has to be chased down
iron-refer.say: If the anemia comes with black or bloody stools, real breathlessness, or weight you didn't mean to lose — get seen promptly so the cause can be found. **This matters most for men and for women past menopause: iron deficiency in either one usually means something is bleeding slowly somewhere, and it has to be tracked down. Topping the iron back up without finding out why is not enough.**

preg-ask-first.label: Everything gets run past the doctor first
preg-ask-first.say: Through pregnancy and nursing I'm a good deal more careful about supplements than usual — not because I don't want to help, but because the safety data for this stretch is genuinely thin. For a lot of ingredients nobody can honestly say 'that's fine for a pregnant woman.' Anything at all — supplements, herbs, teas — run it past the OB or the pharmacist first.

preg-folate.label: Folic acid is the clear one
preg-folate.say: Folic acid is one of the few with a clear, settled recommendation: **the CDC advises 400 micrograms a day for anyone who could become pregnant, starting before you conceive** — the part of the baby it protects forms very early, often before you know you're pregnant. Leafy greens and beans have folate naturally, and most prenatal vitamins already contain it. Exactly what to take is something the OB will sort out at the first visit — they always do.

preg-food-safety.label: The foods to steer clear of
preg-food-safety.say: The list to steer clear of: raw or undercooked fish and eggs, unpasteurized milk and soft cheeses, deli meat and hot dogs unless they're heated through, raw sprouts, the high-mercury fish (shark, swordfish, king mackerel, tilefish), and alcohol. Go easy on caffeine as well — how much is all right for you is a question for the OB.

preg-herbs-caution.label: Herbs and oils count too
preg-herbs-caution.say: 'All natural' does not mean 'safe while pregnant.' Plenty of herbs, herbal teas, traditional remedies and essential oils carry real question marks in pregnancy and nursing. That includes the well-meant tonic somebody's mother brings over — ask first, and don't feel awkward about asking.

preg-rest.label: The tiredness is real
preg-rest.say: The tiredness in this stretch is real tiredness. Sleep when you can and take the day off when you need it — you're doing something that costs the body a great deal. That isn't being precious.

preg-med-blocked.label: Which medicines are safe
preg-med-blocked.say: Which medicines are safe in pregnancy and nursing is something I make no judgment on at all — right down to cold medicine and pain relievers, ask the doctor or the pharmacist. And a long-term medication you were already on: **do not stop it on your own.** That's for the doctor to adjust.

preg-refer.label: The signs that can't wait
preg-refer.say: **Bleeding, belly pain that won't let up, the baby moving noticeably less, or your water breaking — go in right away, don't wait.** Call your OB or head straight for labor and delivery. A bad headache along with blurred vision or sudden swelling can be a warning sign of preeclampsia — that one is right away too. And afterward: if the low mood keeps going and nothing holds any interest, that's postpartum depression — an illness, not a sign you don't love the baby enough. **988 is there any hour of the day, and you can text it as easily as call it.**

tcm-see-doctor.label: Curious about acupuncture? Here's the lay of the land
tcm-see-doctor.say: If you're curious about acupuncture, it's well established in the U.S. — look for a licensed acupuncturist (most states license them). The research support is strongest for certain kinds of pain, chronic low back pain especially. Worth knowing: **Medicare covers acupuncture for chronic low back pain** — up to 12 sessions in 90 days, through Medicare-enrolled providers — and some private plans cover more, so check before paying out of pocket.

tcm-both-lanes.label: Tell both sides what you're taking
tcm-both-lanes.say: If you use herbal or traditional remedies alongside regular medicine, don't keep either side in the dark — **your doctor and your pharmacist both need the full list**. Herbs and prescriptions can genuinely clash, and they can only protect you from that if they know.

tcm-food-warm.label: Gentle kitchen remedies
tcm-food-warm.say: If you like starting gently, start in the kitchen: ginger tea for a queasy stomach, chicken soup when you're run down, chamomile tea in the evening to unwind. These are foods, not medicines — mild, cheap, and comforting — and there's nothing wrong with that.

tcm-routine.label: Routine beats any supplement
tcm-routine.say: On this, traditional wisdom and modern medicine say the exact same thing: sleep on a regular schedule, eat regular meals, keep moving, and don't let stress stew. Get those right and they'll do more for you than anything sold in a bottle — and they're free.

tcm-herb-interaction.label: A few herbs that need real caution
tcm-herb-interaction.dailyCap: I don't give amounts — run any herb past your doctor or pharmacist
tcm-herb-interaction.say: A few specific warnings worth having: **dong quai, found in some menopause and 'women's' herbal blends, can raise bleeding risk if you're on blood thinners**. And **real licorice — black licorice candy, or licorice root in teas and supplements — can push blood pressure up and potassium down** when you have it regularly; the FDA has warned about this, especially for folks over 40. I won't give you amounts for any herb — bring the package to your doctor or pharmacist. And during pregnancy or nursing, herbs are always an ask-first.

tcm-prescribe-blocked.label: Diagnosing and dosing herbs
tcm-prescribe-blocked.say: I can't diagnose you in traditional-medicine terms, pick herbs for you, or tell you how much of one to take — that's for licensed professionals who can actually examine you. And one thing I will never do is tell you to drop a prescription in favor of an herb.

tcm-refer.label: When to stop and see a doctor
tcm-refer.say: If after taking any herbal remedy your skin or the whites of your eyes turn yellow, you swell up, you bruise or bleed for no reason, or you get severe diarrhea or vomiting — **stop taking it and see a doctor promptly**. And the most important line of all: **never stop your prescription medicines to take an herb instead** — especially blood pressure, blood sugar, heart, or blood thinner medication. That risk is never worth it.

lex-b-complex.label: B vitamins / B complex
lex-b-complex.dailyCap: Follow the label; don't take high-dose B6 long term (it can cause nerve damage)
lex-b-complex.say: B vitamins aren't an energy pill — they're helpers for your metabolism. **If you're low, topping up helps; if you're not, you mostly get expensive yellow urine** (that's normal, not proof it's working). Who actually runs low: strict vegetarians and vegans (B12), heavy drinkers, and people on certain long-term stomach-acid medicines. Three things: stick to the label; **high-dose B6 over the long haul can cause numb, tingling hands and feet** — more is not better; and it can interact with Parkinson's medication, so ask the doctor first if that applies.

lex-vitamin-c.label: Vitamin C
lex-vitamin-c.dailyCap: Adult upper limit is 2,000 mg a day (a safety ceiling, not a target)
lex-vitamin-c.say: On vitamin C and colds, the big research reviews are pretty deflating: **taking it regularly doesn't really prevent colds — at best it shaves a little off how long one lasts**. One orange or a cup of strawberries already covers your daily need. If you take it anyway: **stay under 2,000 mg a day** — more than that invites diarrhea — and **if you've had kidney stones, skip the high doses** (it raises oxalate). Fruit is still the better route.

lex-vitamin-d.label: Vitamin D
lex-vitamin-d.dailyCap: Follow the label; it's fat-soluble and builds up — don't stack multiple products that contain D
lex-vitamin-d.say: Plenty of older adults do run low on vitamin D — but here's the honest part: the biggest recent trials found that **for healthy people who aren't deficient, extra D didn't prevent fractures, cancer, or heart disease** the way everyone hoped. Correcting a real deficiency still matters. Sunlight is the cheapest source — ten or fifteen minutes a day helps. If you supplement: **D is fat-soluble and builds up in the body**, so don't stack several products that all contain it. A blood test at your next checkup settles whether you're actually low — just ask.

lex-fish-oil.label: Fish oil (omega-3)
lex-fish-oil.dailyCap: Follow the label; ask your doctor before combining with blood thinners, and stop before surgery
lex-fish-oil.say: The fish oil story needs an update: **in the big recent trials, ordinary fish oil capsules mostly didn't prevent heart attacks or strokes**. (The one that did work is a high-dose prescription version — that comes from a doctor, not the supplement aisle.) What does have good evidence is simpler: **eat fish twice a week**. If you take fish oil anyway, remember **it thins the blood a little — check with your doctor if you're on a blood thinner, and stop it before surgery or dental work**. Fishy burps and an upset stomach are the common complaints.

lex-q10.label: CoQ10
lex-q10.say: People take CoQ10 for two main reasons: heart support (there's some early evidence as an add-on in heart failure — alongside treatment, never instead of it) and the muscle aches from statins (the studies there honestly disagree — it helps some people, does nothing for others). **The line that matters most: CoQ10 can weaken warfarin, the blood thinner** — if you're on it, ask your doctor first, because a quietly weakened blood thinner is a dangerous thing.

lex-turmeric.label: Turmeric (curcumin)
lex-turmeric.dailyCap: Follow the label and don't chase high doses (liver-injury reports cluster at high doses)
lex-turmeric.say: Turmeric — curcumin — has some small studies behind it for achy joints, but the body absorbs it poorly by nature; that's why every brand brags about its special formula. Three cautions: **skip it if you have gallstones** (it makes the gallbladder contract); **it thins the blood** — avoid combining it with blood thinners or taking it before surgery; and **high-dose curcumin has been linked to reported cases of liver injury** — if your liver isn't in great shape, ask a doctor first, and if your skin or eyes ever turn yellow, stop immediately.

lex-cranberry.label: Cranberry
lex-cranberry.dailyCap: Follow the label; never use it in place of a doctor for an active infection
lex-cranberry.say: For **preventing repeat urinary tract infections**, the latest big research review actually came around: it does seem to help certain people — women with recurring UTIs especially. But **once an infection has started, cranberry won't treat it — that needs a doctor**. Two cautions: it interacts with **warfarin, the blood thinner**, and the juice carries a lot of sugar — if you're watching your blood sugar, the pills or a low-sugar version make more sense.

lex-collagen.label: Collagen
lex-collagen.say: Honest answer: collagen gets digested into building blocks like any other protein — **swallowing collagen doesn't ship collagen straight to your skin**. The skin studies show small improvements in moisture and elasticity, but they're small trials and many are industry-funded. Fine to try with 'we'll see' money — not with 'fountain of youth' money. Enough protein, enough vitamin C, and sunscreen all have stronger evidence for your skin. Allergic to fish or shellfish? Check the source on the label.

lex-probiotic.label: Probiotics
lex-probiotic.dailyCap: Follow the label; don't stack several similar products at once
lex-probiotic.say: With probiotics, everything depends on **which strain, for what problem** — no one bottle does it all. The evidence is better for digestive troubles than for 'immune boosting,' and what worked for your neighbor may do nothing for you. Three things: **space them two hours apart from antibiotics** (or they're wasted); **if your immune system is compromised or you're in cancer treatment, don't take them without asking your doctor**; and if a month or two brings no difference, stop — no loyalty to a bottle.

lex-multivitamin.label: Multivitamins
lex-multivitamin.dailyCap: One a day, and don't stack it on top of single-ingredient supplements
lex-multivitamin.say: Honest answer: the large studies keep coming back the same way — **a daily multivitamin makes little to no difference for preventing chronic disease or living longer**. Its reasonable job is filling gaps when eating has gotten spotty; it's not insurance and it's not treatment. If you take one: one a day, and **don't stack it on top of separate calcium, D, or B pills** — the fat-soluble ones build up. Money you want to spend on health buys more at the grocery store than at the vitamin shelf.

lex-ginseng.label: Ginseng
lex-ginseng.dailyCap: Don't make it a daily long-term habit; if you're on regular medications, ask first
lex-ginseng.say: Ginseng has a long list of medicines it argues with: **blood thinners, diabetes medicines (it can push blood sugar too low), and some blood pressure pills**. Skip it when you're sick with a fever, and it winds some people up — worse sleep, feeling overheated. If you take any regular medication, run it past your pharmacist before starting.

lex-lingzhi.label: Reishi mushroom
lex-lingzhi.dailyCap: Follow the label — and treat any 'treats disease' claim as marketing
lex-lingzhi.say: Reishi's immune research is still at an early stage — and **any 'fights cancer' claim you see is marketing, not human evidence**. Two hard rules: **it affects blood clotting** — avoid it with blood thinners and before surgery; and **if you're on immune-suppressing drugs** (organ transplant, autoimmune treatment) **don't take it** — it pushes in the opposite direction from your medication.

lex-melatonin.label: Melatonin
lex-melatonin.say: Melatonin is sold right on the shelf here, so let me give you the straight story. Where it genuinely helps: **jet lag and a body clock that's shifted off schedule** — that's what the evidence supports, for short-term use. For plain chronic insomnia, **the American Academy of Sleep Medicine actually advises against it** — the evidence is too weak. One more honest wrinkle: **store-bought melatonin is famously inconsistent** — when researchers lab-tested melatonin gummies, most contained far more or less than the label claimed. If you try it: keep it short-term, mention it to your pharmacist (it can interact with blood thinners and other medicines), and if sleep has been bad for months, the better road is a talk with your doctor — there's a non-drug therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) with much stronger evidence.

lex-one-at-a-time.label: One at a time, with a deadline
lex-one-at-a-time.say: Two rules when trying any new supplement: **add only one at a time** (otherwise you'll never know which one did what), and **give it a deadline** — if a month or two brings nothing you can feel, stop. I can remember the start date for you and check back in.

lex-pharmacist.label: Take the whole bag to the pharmacist
lex-pharmacist.say: If your pills and supplements together number more than five, here's the most practical move there is: **bring the whole bag to your pharmacy and ask for a medication review**. If you're on a Medicare drug plan, you may qualify for a free yearly review — it's called Medication Therapy Management, just ask. A pharmacist can spot two bottles that fight each other at a glance.

lex-refer.label: When to stop and get help
lex-refer.say: After starting any supplement, if your skin or the whites of your eyes turn yellow, you break out in a rash or swell up, your heart races, or your muscles ache and feel weak — **stop taking it and see a doctor promptly**, and bring the bottle with you. And the most important rule of all: **never stop a prescription medicine in favor of a supplement** — that trade is never worth the risk.  And if your lips or eyelids swell, you break out in hives, or you have trouble breathing — that can be anaphylaxis. Don't wait; call 911.

lex-drug-clash.label: The combinations that genuinely cause harm
lex-drug-clash.say: These are the pairs worth memorizing. **Blood thinners × fish oil, ginkgo, concentrated garlic, turmeric, nattokinase** — bleeding risk stacks. **Cholesterol medication × red yeast rice** — the same mechanism twice, with a risk of muscle breakdown. **Diabetes medication × anything marketed for blood sugar** (berberine, bitter melon) — you can go too low. **Thyroid medication × calcium or iron** — absorption is blocked; keep them four hours apart. **Diuretics × licorice-containing products** — potassium drops. **St. John's wort × a long list** — including blood thinners, antidepressants and some heart medications. The response to all of it is the same one thing: **before starting anything new, show every bottle to a pharmacist.** It's free and it's the most reliable check there is.

lex-stop-med.label: Can I stop my medication and take a supplement instead?
lex-stop-med.say: That isn't mine to decide, and it shouldn't be. But one thing is clear. **Don't stop a prescribed medicine on your own in order to take a supplement.** Blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol all progress silently — "I felt fine so I stopped" shows up months later, and sometimes it can't be undone. That said, three things are yours. **One: wanting fewer medications is a legitimate thing to say out loud to your doctor.** Don't hide it. **Two: bring numbers.** Home blood pressure readings, weight changes — whether anything can come down is decided on that evidence. **Three: if something can be reduced, it comes down in steps, with checks.** Some medications rebound badly if stopped abruptly.

lex-lutein.label: Lutein
lex-lutein.dailyCap: Typically 10 mg a day. Smokers should avoid eye formulas containing high-dose beta-carotene
lex-lutein.say: Lutein has real evidence in **people who already have intermediate or advanced macular degeneration** — as part of a specific formula, it slows progression. That part is genuine. But **there's weak evidence that a person with healthy eyes benefits from taking it "to prevent" anything, or for screen fatigue.** I'd rather say that plainly. Most tired eyes come from not blinking enough and holding the screen too close. Look 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes, brighten the room, put the screen slightly below eye level — free, and more reliable. One safety point: **if you smoke, avoid eye formulas with high-dose beta-carotene** — that combination raises lung cancer risk.

lex-calcium.label: Calcium
lex-calcium.dailyCap: No more than 500 mg at a time from supplements; total from food and pills 1000 to 1200 mg a day
lex-calcium.say: Calcium is a **food-first** nutrient — dairy, canned sardines, tofu set with calcium, kale, fortified alternatives. Supplements fill the gap, they don't replace the plate. From pills, **take no more than 500 mg at once** — the body can only absorb so much at a time, and excess drives constipation and kidney stones. Keep the total from food and supplements to 1000 to 1200 mg a day. **You need adequate vitamin D for calcium to be absorbed**, so get sun or take D alongside. Keep it **four hours** from thyroid medication, iron, and some antibiotics. If you've had kidney stones or been told your blood calcium is high, ask before starting.

lex-iron-zinc.label: Iron and zinc — only if you're low, and too much does damage
lex-iron-zinc.dailyCap: Both only after a blood test confirms a deficiency. Zinc: don't exceed 40 mg a day long-term
lex-iron-zinc.say: These two are strictly "only if you're low." **If you're not deficient there's no benefit, and there is harm.** **Iron** — don't take it long-term without being told you're anemic. Excess iron accumulates and damages the liver and other organs. When you do take it: an hour away from tea and coffee, and with vitamin C for better absorption. Black stools are expected, but **they can't be told apart from gastrointestinal bleeding**, so always say "I'm on iron" at any visit. **Zinc** — it comes up for loss of taste or slow wound healing, but sustained doses above 40 mg a day cause copper deficiency and a different problem. For both, the first step is a blood test, not a bottle.

supp-konjac-fiber.label: Konjac / glucomannan fiber
supp-konjac-fiber.dailyCap: Around 3 g a day. Always with a full glass of water, and never right before lying down
supp-konjac-fiber.say: Glucomannan from konjac swells with water, so there's modest evidence for fullness and cholesterol. For weight, any effect is small. **The important part is how you take it safely.** Powders and capsules go down **with a full glass of water**, and **never right before lying down or going to bed**. Without enough fluid it can swell in the throat or esophagus and obstruct — that has genuinely happened to people. Don't use it if swallowing is difficult or you've been told the esophagus is narrowed. **Keep it two hours from other medications.** And konjac jelly candies are a choking hazard — cut them small for older adults and children.

lex-glucosamine.label: Glucosamine (the knee bottle)
lex-glucosamine.dailyCap: Usually 1500 mg a day. Try three months; if nothing changes, stop
lex-glucosamine.say: One of the best-selling supplements with some of the shakiest evidence. Pooling the large trials, **overall it's close to no different from placebo.** A few reports suggest a small edge in people with more severe pain, but nothing dependable. So treat it this way: trying it is your call, but **give it three months, and if you can't tell a difference yourself, stop and spend the money elsewhere.** This isn't something to take for five years on faith. What the money reliably buys instead: strengthening the front of the thigh, and losing a kilogram — the knee carries several times your body weight with every step. Many products are shellfish-derived, so check the label for a shellfish allergy. If you have diabetes, keep an eye on your numbers.

lex-red-yeast-rice.label: Red yeast rice
lex-red-yeast-rice.dailyCap: Do not combine with a prescription cholesterol medication
lex-red-yeast-rice.say: Red yeast rice naturally contains essentially the same compound as prescription cholesterol drugs. "Natural" does not mean mild here. **Taken alongside a prescription cholesterol medication, it risks muscle breakdown that can damage the kidneys.** The amount varies enormously between products, and the label won't tell you how strong yours actually is — some contain almost none, some contain a full drug dose. Avoid it if you're pregnant, breastfeeding, or have liver problems. If you're taking it, **bring the bottle to your next appointment**. Saying nothing is the dangerous choice.

lex-nattokinase.label: Nattokinase
lex-nattokinase.dailyCap: Follow the label. Not with blood thinners without medical advice; stop 14 days before surgery
lex-nattokinase.say: Nattokinase is sold to "thin the blood," and there is some laboratory basis for that — which is exactly why it deserves caution rather than enthusiasm. **On top of a blood thinner or anti-platelet medicine it raises bleeding risk**, and there's no good evidence that it prevents strokes or heart attacks the way prescribed medicine does. Here's the twist worth knowing: **natto the food does the opposite** in one respect — it's very high in vitamin K, which works against warfarin. So the supplement and the food pull in different directions, and neither should be added casually if you're on a blood thinner. Stop it at least 14 days before any surgery or dental extraction, and tell the surgeon.

lex-ginkgo.label: Ginkgo biloba
lex-ginkgo.dailyCap: Usually 120 to 240 mg a day. Stop 14 days before surgery or dental work
lex-ginkgo.say: Ginkgo is sold for memory, tinnitus and circulation. Honestly, **the evidence is weak for all three.** A large prevention trial found no effect on dementia. For tinnitus, pooled results are close to no difference. And the cautions are clear: **it adds to bleeding risk with blood thinners**, **it may lower the seizure threshold in people with epilepsy**, and it should be **stopped 14 days before surgery or dental extraction**. If memory is the worry, that money is better spent on your hearing, your blood pressure, your sleep, and time spent with other people — all of which have stronger evidence than any bottle.

lex-maca.label: Maca and royal jelly
lex-maca.dailyCap: Follow the label. Ask first if you've had a hormone-related cancer
lex-maca.say: Maca is sold for energy and for "that department." The studies are small and the support is thin — fine as a food, disappointing as a miracle. **Royal jelly carries one safety point I have to make.** There are a number of reported cases of severe allergic reactions, asthma attacks and anaphylaxis after taking it, and almost all occurred in people who already had asthma, hay fever or eczema. I don't recommend it for anyone with that background. If you're going to try it anyway, take a tiny amount the first time, with someone nearby — and if your throat tightens, your lips swell, hives appear, or breathing gets hard, **call 911 immediately**. For both: **if you've had a hormone-related cancer such as breast or prostate, ask your doctor first** — how they act on hormones isn't well understood. If you actually want energy back, check three things first: hours of sleep, whether you get outside and move during the day, and whether anemia or a thyroid problem has been missed. Those beat any bottle.

lex-bitter-melon.label: Bitter melon, berberine and the blood-sugar supplements
lex-bitter-melon.dailyCap: Not a substitute for diabetes medication. Berberine interacts with many drugs — ask first
lex-bitter-melon.say: **None of these replaces diabetes medication**, and that's the sentence that matters most. **Bitter melon** — pooled trials found no measurable advantage over placebo, and the studies were low quality. Great as a vegetable, not as a treatment. **Berberine** does lower glucose in small studies — which is precisely why it isn't harmless. **Stacked on diabetes medication it can drop you too low**, and it interacts with a long list of drugs, including some blood thinners and blood pressure medicines. It's also not for pregnancy or breastfeeding. If you want to try something, tell the doctor who manages your diabetes before you start, add only one thing at a time, and check your numbers more often for the first two weeks.

lex-essence-chicken.label: Chicken essence, bone broth and "liver support" drinks
lex-essence-chicken.dailyCap: Watch the sodium; skip if you have gout, high uric acid, or are on dialysis
lex-essence-chicken.say: These get sold as a pick-me-up for someone who's run down, and as gifts to the sick. Here's the honest accounting. **A serving contains less usable protein than a single egg**, and costs many times more. If someone genuinely needs protein, an egg, a cup of milk or a piece of fish does more for less. As for "liver support" and "detox" claims — **the liver and kidneys already do that job**, and no drink improves on them. What actually protects the liver is less alcohol, a healthy weight, and not layering on unlabeled herbal products. Two groups should skip these: **gout or high uric acid** (purine load), and **anyone on dialysis or with reduced kidney function** (protein and potassium). Many are also high in sodium, which matters with high blood pressure. If it's a comfort ritual with family, that has its own value — just don't let it stand in for real food or real treatment.

lipid-numbers-blocked.label: Reading your numbers, and changing the dose
lipid-numbers-blocked.say: What your cholesterol numbers mean, whether you need medicine, and whether a dose should change — that's the doctor's call, made against your whole risk picture: your age, your blood pressure, whether you have diabetes, whether you smoke. I don't read numbers and I don't touch doses. What I can do is help you hold up the living end of it.

lipid-statin-dont-stop.label: Never stop your statin on your own
lipid-statin-dont-stop.say: First, and it's the important one: **don't stop your statin on your own.** High cholesterol doesn't feel like anything, so plenty of people see a good number on the lab report and figure they're done — but the number is good *because* of the pill. Stopping it, or quietly skipping days, is your doctor's decision to make, not an experiment to run at home. If it's the cost or a side effect bothering you, say so at the appointment; there's usually another way.

lipid-fiber.label: Fiber, especially oats and beans
lipid-fiber.say: The soluble fiber in oatmeal, beans, barley, apples and psyllium grabs some of the cholesterol in your gut and carries it out the door — it's the best-evidenced thing on your plate for the bad cholesterol, solid enough that the FDA lets oat boxes say so. Trading the white toast for a bowl of oatmeal at breakfast is one plain step you can take tomorrow.

lipid-fat-swap.label: Swapping the fat beats fearing all fat
lipid-fat-swap.say: The point isn't to strip the fat out of your food — it's **which** fat. Less deep-fried, less of what's in pastries, biscuits and packaged baked goods; more olive oil, nuts and fish. The same calories on the plate, different numbers on the lab report.

lipid-move.label: Regular aerobic exercise
lipid-move.say: Brisk walking, swimming, riding a bike — that kind of steady movement does the most for **your triglycerides and your good cholesterol.** The bad cholesterol mostly answers to food and medicine; those two answer to your legs. Half an hour, five days a week is the usual target, and it still counts broken into ten-minute pieces.

lipid-tg-alcohol-sugar.label: If it's the triglycerides, start with alcohol and sugar
lipid-tg-alcohol-sugar.say: If the number that's high is your **triglycerides** rather than your cholesterol, the two things that move it most are cutting back on alcohol and cutting the sweet drinks and white starches. This one answers to food much faster than cholesterol does — two or three months and you can usually see it on the next lab report.

lipid-red-yeast-caution.label: Red yeast rice isn't a free add-on
lipid-red-yeast-caution.dailyCap: Ask your doctor or pharmacist before taking it alongside a prescription cholesterol medicine — don't set a dose for yourself
lipid-red-yeast-caution.say: Red yeast rice naturally contains the same kind of compound as a statin drug — so **taking it on top of a prescription statin is a double dose of the same thing**, and that's how people end up with serious muscle damage. It's sold as a supplement, too, which means how much is really in the bottle varies a lot from brand to brand. If you want to try it, ask the pharmacist first, and never use it as a substitute for the medicine you were prescribed.

lipid-normalize.label: There's nothing to feel, and that's normal
lipid-normalize.say: High cholesterol almost never announces itself — no ache, no warning sign. That's why most people find out from a blood test at a checkup rather than from feeling anything. It isn't that you weren't paying attention to your body; there was nothing there to notice.

lipid-refer.label: The muscle sign, and the chest sign
lipid-refer.say: Two things to know. **If you're on a statin and you get unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness — especially all over, or along with feeling sick or feverish, or if your urine turns dark brown like tea — stop the statin and get seen right away.** That's the one exception to never stopping on your own: rarely, muscle can break down and injure the kidneys. And the reason cholesterol matters at all is the heart: **chest pressure or chest pain with a cold sweat means call 911 now** and treat it as the heart until someone proves otherwise. Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes also needs to be looked at.

wt-unintended-loss.label: First: did you mean to lose it?
wt-unintended-loss.say: Before anything else, one question that matters: is this weight loss **something you set out to do** — or did it just happen? If it happened on its own — noticeably lighter over the last six months, pants getting loose, no dieting behind it — that isn't good news, and I'm not going to congratulate you for it. Weight that leaves without being asked is usually the body saying something else, and it's worth having a doctor find out what.

wt-waist-first.label: The tape measure tells you more than the scale
wt-waist-first.say: The number on the scale can fool you — muscle weighs, water weighs. **Your waist is the better measure.** Run a tape measure around your middle at the belly button: over 40 inches for a man, over 35 for a woman is the line American doctors use for too much fat packed in around the organs. (If you're of Asian background, ask your doctor — the useful line sits lower.) One minute with a tape tells you more than stepping on the scale does.

wt-metabolic-syndrome.label: Metabolic syndrome — they travel in a group
wt-metabolic-syndrome.say: A thick waist, blood pressure creeping up, blood sugar creeping up, high triglycerides, low good cholesterol — **any three of those five together is what's called metabolic syndrome.** It isn't a disease so much as a warning light. The lines used here are a waist over 40 inches for men or 35 for women, triglycerides at 150 or above, good cholesterol under 40 for men or under 50 for women, blood pressure at 130/85 or above (or already being treated), and a fasting blood sugar of 100 or above. Pull out your last lab report, count how many you've collected, and take that count to your doctor.

wt-sugar-drinks.label: The sweet drinks go first
wt-sugar-drinks.say: If you're only going to change one thing, make it the sweet drinks — soda, sweet tea, juice, sports drinks, the big flavored coffees. Sugar you drink doesn't fill you up, and it lands around the middle faster than anything else. Plenty of people watch their waist change from that one swap alone.

wt-slow-is-right.label: Slow is what actually stays off
wt-slow-is-right.say: Two to four pounds a month is the pace that holds. Weight that comes off faster than that is mostly water and muscle, and it comes back the moment you stop — and muscle an older body gives up is hard to put back on. **This is one thing you can't hurry.**

wt-fatty-liver.label: Fatty liver: the treatment is weight, not a pill
wt-fatty-liver.say: Fatty liver turns up on a great many scans — you may see it written the newer way now, MASLD. Here's the useful part: **losing five to ten percent of your body weight visibly clears fat back out of the liver**, which makes this one of the few conditions where changing how you live *is* the real treatment. There is now one prescription drug for the advanced form, but that's a liver specialist's decision, not a first step. Skip the liver-support supplements; cutting the sugar and the alcohol does far more.

wt-muscle-not-just-diet.label: Eating less alone takes the muscle with it
wt-muscle-not-just-diet.say: If the only thing you do is eat less, part of what comes off is muscle — more so as we get older. Get enough protein and add something with resistance in it (standing up out of a chair and sitting back down, lifting a jug of water), and what you lose will be the fat.

wt-diet-pills-blocked.label: Weight-loss pills and the shots
wt-diet-pills-blocked.say: Whether a weight-loss medication — including the shots everybody's talking about — is right for you is a conversation between you and a doctor who knows your history. I won't tell you whether you're a candidate, and I don't discuss doses. Two honest things I will say: this is a real prescription route, so it's worth raising at your next appointment instead of wondering about it; and **stay away from compounded or online-sourced versions.** The FDA has logged people hospitalized after measuring the wrong amount out of those vials, and counterfeits are circulating. If you go this way, go through a licensed prescriber and a real pharmacy.

wt-refer.label: The weight changes that need a doctor
wt-refer.say: **Unexplained weight loss gets checked out, not celebrated** — noticeably lighter over six months or so with no diet behind it, especially alongside appetite falling off, trouble swallowing, night sweats, or black or bloody stools. Thyroid trouble, stomach and bowel problems, and cancer all show up this way, and the point of going in is to rule them out. It runs the other direction too: weight climbing quickly along with swelling in the legs and getting more short of breath is a heart and kidney question, not ordinary weight gain. Either one, get seen.

diet-mediterranean.label: The Mediterranean way has the sturdiest evidence
diet-mediterranean.say: If you want the one with real long-term evidence behind it, it's the Mediterranean pattern: vegetables and fruit, whole grains, beans, nuts, olive oil, fish a couple of times a week, and less red meat. The heart research behind it is the strongest of any way of eating — and just as important, **it doesn't ask you to give anything up entirely, so people stay on it.** In an American kitchen that looks like: vegetables on the plate first, olive oil instead of butter, half the white bread and rice traded for whole grain, and fish showing up more often than beef.

diet-dash.label: If blood pressure is the problem, start with DASH
diet-dash.say: For anyone whose blood pressure is the issue, DASH is where to start — **more potassium from fruit and vegetables, more calcium, less sodium.** It was built for blood pressure, and the evidence is clear-cut. One caution: if your kidneys aren't in good shape, don't go loading up on potassium-rich foods without asking your doctor first.

diet-low-carb-honest.label: Low-carb: fast at first, even later
diet-low-carb-honest.say: Straight talk: low-carb usually takes weight off faster in the first six months, but **a year or two out it comes out about the same as the other approaches** — what separates them is whether you can keep it up. Keto, the strict version, is harder to live with for long. And **if you take medicine for blood sugar, cutting carbs on your own can drop you too low** — that one goes past your doctor first, because the medicine may need to change along with the food. If you want to try it, start with one less serving of rice, bread or pasta and one more of vegetables. Don't jump to the far end.

diet-fasting-honest.label: Intermittent fasting isn't magic — it's another way of eating less
diet-fasting-honest.say: Where the research lands on intermittent fasting: **it works about the same as simply eating that much less** — there's no special metabolic trick in it. What it does have going for it is one simple rule, and some people find a rule easier to follow than counting. But **don't take it on by yourself if you're on blood sugar medicine, if you're pregnant or nursing, or if you've ever had an eating disorder.** And older folks deserve extra care here: if you're already eating lightly, squeezing meals into a short window is an easy way to come up short on protein.

diet-pick-what-you-can-keep.label: The best one is the one you'll still be doing in three months
diet-pick-what-you-can-keep.say: Line all the diets up honestly and the strongest one turns out to be **the one you'll actually keep doing** — the research finds that over and over. So rather than asking which is most powerful, ask which one you'd still be following three months from now. Tell me how you eat these days and we'll adjust from there instead of starting you over.

diet-detox-blocked.label: Detoxes, cleanses and juice fasts
diet-detox-blocked.say: 'Detox' isn't a real thing in medicine — your liver and kidneys do that work around the clock, and a cleanse doesn't help them do it. The extreme versions, days of nothing but juice, can throw your electrolytes off, which is genuinely risky if you take heart or blood pressure medicine. I won't recommend them.

diet-refer.label: When a change in eating needs a doctor
diet-refer.say: If you change how you're eating and get shaky, sweaty and lightheaded — **especially if you take medicine for blood sugar** — treat it as low blood sugar: juice or glucose tablets right away, then get advice about your doses. And one line that isn't up for negotiation: **don't drop a prescribed medicine to make a diet work.** If an older person starts eating less and less and keeps getting thinner, that isn't a diet succeeding — that needs a doctor. Same goes for dieting hard enough that periods stop or hair starts coming out.

allergy-vs-intolerance.label: An allergy and an intolerance are two different things
allergy-vs-intolerance.say: Let's sort out which one we're talking about, because they're handled completely differently. **An allergy is the immune system**: hives, swelling lips, wheezing, and at worst a whole-body reaction — and a tiny amount can set it off. **An intolerance is digestion** — milk leaving you gassy and running to the bathroom is the classic one: miserable, but not life-threatening, and a small amount is usually fine. Which of those sounds like yours?

allergy-record.label: Write down what, how long after, and what happened
allergy-record.say: If you suspect a food, the most useful thing you can do is keep a record: what you ate, how long before it started, what happened, and how long it lasted. Handing a doctor that list beats guessing by a mile — and I can hold onto it for you if you tell me as it happens.

allergy-label.label: Reading the label: the nine the US requires
allergy-label.say: Packaged food sold here has to spell out nine major allergens: **milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans — and sesame, which was added at the start of 2023.** Look for the 'Contains' line right under the ingredient list; that's the fastest place to check. Turning the box over before it goes in the cart is a lot easier than dealing with it afterward.

allergy-lactose.label: Lactose intolerance: you don't have to give up dairy
allergy-lactose.say: Milk leaving you bloated and headed for the bathroom is usually lactose intolerance rather than an allergy — and **you don't have to quit dairy over it.** Yogurt and aged cheeses carry much less lactose, lactose-free milk is in every grocery store, small amounts alongside a meal go down better, and the lactase tablets at the drugstore help some people. Just don't let the calcium slide while you're cutting back.

allergy-no-self-elimination.label: Don't put yourself on a long avoid list
allergy-no-self-elimination.say: Cutting out a whole list of foods on a hunch is riskier than it sounds — **especially for an older person**, where it quietly turns into not eating enough and losing weight. If something really does need to come out, do it with a doctor or a dietitian, one food at a time, rather than crossing things off month after month on your own.

allergy-test-blocked.label: 'Food sensitivity' panels (IgG testing)
allergy-test-blocked.say: You'll see clinics and websites selling 'food sensitivity' panels — usually IgG testing — promising a list of everything you can't eat. **Allergy specialists advise against using those to decide what to avoid**: IgG mostly reflects what you've been eating, not what you react to, and the lists they hand back send people off a dozen foods for no good reason. If you want a real answer, see a board-certified allergist and let them choose the test that fits your story. I won't recommend a lab or interpret a panel for you.

allergy-refer.label: The reaction that's an airway emergency
allergy-refer.say: **This is the one that matters most. If after eating, the lips or tongue swell, the throat feels tight, the voice goes hoarse, breathing turns hard or wheezy, or hives break out all over along with dizziness — that's a severe allergic reaction closing off the airway. Call 911 right now. Don't wait it out, and don't drive yourself.** If an epinephrine auto-injector has been prescribed, use it first and then call. And anyone who has ever reacted that way should ask their doctor about carrying one — that conversation belongs on the calendar, not in the middle of an emergency.

sarco-what-it-looks-like.label: The signs worth watching aren't on the scale
sarco-what-it-looks-like.say: As the years go by, **too little muscle causes more trouble than too much weight does.** The signs to watch: the jar lid you can't twist open anymore, groceries that suddenly feel heavy, needing to push off the armrests to stand up, and walking slowly enough that the crosswalk light beats you across. Any of those and it's time to start — you don't need a diagnosis first.

sarco-protein-每餐.label: Protein at every meal, not all at dinner
sarco-protein-每餐.say: A lot of older folks have toast and coffee for breakfast and get all their protein at supper — but **the body can only use so much of it at once.** Put a serving in every meal instead: an egg, a cup of milk, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, beans, tofu, or a palm-sized piece of fish or chicken. Same food overall, far more muscle out of it. Older adults generally need more protein than the old textbook number — the researchers land around 25 to 30 grams a meal — though **if your kidneys aren't in good shape, that number is your doctor's or a dietitian's to set, not mine.**

sarco-resistance.label: Strength work beats another walk
sarco-resistance.say: Walking is good for you, but **muscle only grows against resistance**: standing up out of a chair and sitting back down ten times holding the back of it, lifting a jug of water up and down, push-ups against the wall, a resistance band. Two or three times a week does more than any amount of extra walking. This is the most basic fall prevention there is.

sarco-sun-vitd.label: Daylight and vitamin D
sarco-sun-vitd.say: People who run low on vitamin D tend to be weaker, too. Fifteen or twenty minutes outside most days — and walk a little while you're out there — is the cheapest thing on this whole list.

sarco-protein-supp.label: Whey and protein powders
sarco-protein-supp.dailyCap: Follow the product label; if your kidneys aren't in good shape, how much protein you get in a day is your doctor's or dietitian's call, not the label's
sarco-protein-supp.say: A protein shake is a fair way to fill the gap when someone honestly can't eat enough — but **on its own, without the strength work, it doesn't build much.** And **if your kidneys aren't in good shape, or you're on dialysis, don't add protein on your own**; that total has to be worked out with your doctor or a dietitian. Food first is the better road anyway: eggs, milk, yogurt, fish, beans.

sarco-appetite.label: Not eating is the root of it
sarco-appetite.say: Most older folks who don't eat enough aren't refusing food — their teeth hurt, they're afraid of choking, or eating alone has taken the appetite out of it. **Fix those first and the protein follows**: get the teeth or the dentures looked at, cook the meat softer and cut it smaller, and find someone to share the table with.

sarco-refer.label: When it isn't just muscle
sarco-refer.say: If someone has **lost a noticeable amount of weight over the past six months without trying to**, that needs a doctor to find the reason — don't file it under muscle loss and leave it there. And a recent fall, or walking that's turned suddenly unsteady, should be looked at soon. A fall is the event that changes everything for an older person, and this is the part where you can still get ahead of it.

ckd-stage-decides-everything.label: What stage you're at changes the answer
ckd-stage-decides-everything.say: Kidney advice sounds like it argues with itself, and that's because **it does — the eating changes at every stage, and in a couple of places it flips over completely.** Before dialysis, most people are asked to go easy on protein. Once dialysis starts, that reverses and the job becomes getting enough of it. The reason what you read online contradicts what your neighbor tells you is that nobody says which stage they're talking about. **Your last lab report — your eGFR — and the stage your doctor put you at are the only honest place to start.** If you're not sure which stage you're at, make that the first question at your next visit.

ckd-salt-substitute-danger.label: Salt substitutes are dangerous for kidney patients
ckd-salt-substitute-danger.say: Here's the one most people have never been told: **those 'lite salt' and 'salt substitute' shakers — Lite Salt, No Salt, Nu-Salt — are mostly potassium chloride.** For healthy kidneys that's usually a good trade. **But kidneys that aren't working well can't clear potassium, and too much of it leaves you weak all over and can throw your heart rhythm off. That's the kind that lands people in the hospital.** Worth knowing too: several common blood pressure medicines push potassium up on their own — the -pril and -sartan ones, and spironolactone. **So if your kidneys aren't in good shape, ask your doctor or pharmacist before you switch shakers.** To cut back on salt safely, lean on garlic, onion, lemon, vinegar, black pepper and the salt-free herb blends instead — that's far safer than swapping one shaker for another.

ckd-potassium-cooking.label: Boil the vegetables, go easy on the broth
ckd-potassium-cooking.say: Potassium dissolves into water, so **boiling vegetables in plenty of water and pouring that water off takes a fair amount of it out** — it works best on potatoes, and better still if you cut them small and soak them first. The other side of that coin: soups, stews, chili and the liquid at the bottom of the pot are exactly where the potassium ended up. Eat the solids, go easy on the broth. **Whether you need to be strict about any of this depends on what your blood work says — that's a question for your doctor or a kidney dietitian, not something to guess at.**

ckd-phosphorus-is-hidden.label: The phosphorus that causes trouble is added, not natural
ckd-phosphorus-is-hidden.say: Phosphorus isn't just in meat and beans. **The troublesome kind is what gets added at the factory — and your body takes up nearly all of it, where the phosphorus in real food comes in around half.** It's in deli meat and 'enhanced' chicken (the package says something about a solution added), colas and other dark sodas, processed cheese, non-dairy creamer, instant puddings, and plenty of packaged baked goods. **Read the ingredient list and look for the letters PHOS** — phosphoric acid, sodium phosphate, calcium phosphate. Manufacturers aren't required to put the amount on the Nutrition Facts panel, so the ingredient list is the only place it shows at all.

ckd-painkillers.label: The drugstore pain aisle is the quiet one
ckd-painkillers.say: Reaching for whatever's in the cabinet when the back or the knees ache is the most common hidden hit the kidneys take. **The ones to watch are the anti-inflammatories — ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) and naproxen (Aleve) — and they hide inside a lot of combination cold, sinus and 'PM' products, so people take them without knowing.** You don't have to sort out which is which. **Say this at the pharmacy counter: 'I have kidney disease — is this okay for my kidneys?'** Say the same sentence to your dentist and to any doctor who's new to you. The pharmacist will hand you something else, and it costs you nothing to ask.

ckd-unknown-herbs.label: The danger is not knowing what's in it
ckd-unknown-herbs.say: This isn't about herbal medicine as such — **it's about not knowing what's actually in the jar.** In this country, supplements and herbal products don't get reviewed by the FDA before they go on the shelf; no one checks the label is true. **And it isn't a theoretical worry: the FDA has had to warn people off botanical products found to contain aristolochic acid, which does permanent kidney damage — some of those people ended up on dialysis.** A licensed practitioner and a sealed product from a reputable maker is one thing. A bag of powder from a market stall, something a relative brought back from a trip, or pills off a website with no ingredient list is another thing entirely. **Look for a USP or NSF seal, and take the actual bottle to your kidney doctor** — they would far rather look at it now than find out later.

ckd-protein-ask-dietitian.label: Protein isn't a case of the less the better
ckd-protein-ask-dietitian.say: People hear 'go easy on protein' and quit meat altogether — then the weight comes off, the strength goes, and they end up falling. **That does the kidneys no good whatsoever.** What you want is the right amount of good-quality protein, and that number is something a person has to work out for you. **Here's the part most people don't know: Medicare pays for that. It's called Medical Nutrition Therapy — three hours with a registered dietitian in your first year and two hours a year after that, at no cost to you, for kidney disease that isn't on dialysis yet. It takes a referral from your doctor, so ask for it by name.** If you're already on dialysis, there's a dietitian on the team at your center — that's what they're there for.

ckd-bp-sugar-is-the-kidney.label: Blood pressure and blood sugar are kidney care
ckd-bp-sugar-is-the-kidney.say: **Diabetes and high blood pressure are the two leading causes of kidney failure in this country** — between them they account for most of it. So taking those pills on schedule, checking your numbers at home and writing them down sounds like it has nothing to do with kidneys. It is, in fact, the most useful kidney care there is. **And if you're on one of the -pril or -sartan blood pressure medicines, it's doing double duty — part of the reason it was picked is to protect the kidneys, not just the pressure.** That's worth remembering on the days you feel fine and wonder why you're still taking anything.

ckd-anemia-is-different.label: Kidney anemia doesn't usually answer to iron pills
ckd-anemia-is-different.say: Anemia is common when kidneys are struggling, but **the usual reason isn't low iron — it's that the kidneys make a hormone that tells the marrow to produce blood, and damaged kidneys make less of it.** So a bottle of iron off the shelf often doesn't lift it, and iron you don't need isn't harmless. This kind of anemia has its own treatments: iron given by IV, and shots that do the job that hormone used to do. **Say it plainly at your next appointment — 'I'm tired all the time and people tell me I look pale' — and ask them to check the blood count and your iron.**

ckd-dialysis-not-the-end.label: If dialysis is coming, planning early changes everything
ckd-dialysis-not-the-end.say: Nobody wants to hear the word, so the conversation gets pushed off until someone can't breathe, ends up in the ER, and starts that same night through a catheter in the neck. **That is the hardest possible way to begin, and it's the route that carries the most infections.** With a few months' notice instead, a fistula can be made in your arm and given time to mature, or you can look at peritoneal dialysis, which is done at home and often runs overnight while you sleep. Some people get evaluated for a transplant before dialysis ever starts. **Medicare covers six kidney-disease education sessions once you're at stage 4 — that is precisely what they're for.** Whether to start, and when, is a conversation you sit down and have. It isn't a sentence handed down to you.

ckd-kidney-supplements-blocked.label: Nothing on a supplement shelf repairs kidneys
ckd-kidney-supplements-blocked.say: Straight answer: **nothing sold as a supplement brings back kidney function that's already been lost.** The products advertised as a 'kidney cleanse' or 'kidney detox' are the ones I'd steer you away from hardest — nobody checks what's in them before they're sold, the amounts aren't reliable, and **damaged kidneys are exactly the ones that can't clear whatever extra is in there.** Some of them are heavy on potassium or phosphorus, which is the last thing you need. Your money and your effort go a great deal further aimed at blood pressure, blood sugar, and staying out of the drugstore anti-inflammatories.

ckd-refer.label: What not to wait on
ckd-refer.say: Don't hold these until the next appointment: **passing much less urine than usual, swelling that comes on fast or weight jumping several pounds in a few days, or feeling weak all over with your heartbeat feeling wrong** — that last one can be potassium, and it needs same-day blood work. **And if you're short of breath lying down and can only sleep sitting up, or someone becomes confused, call 911.** That's fluid backing up, and it isn't something to sleep on and see about in the morning.

lung-controller-vs-reliever.label: Two inhalers, two completely different jobs
lung-controller-vs-reliever.say: If the doctor sent you home with two inhalers, **they are not two versions of the same thing.** One is the daily maintenance inhaler — the controller — and it works slowly, calming the swelling inside the airways over weeks. The other is the rescue inhaler, for the moments you can't get your breath. **Nearly everybody makes the same mistake: the rescue inhaler lives in the pocket, and the controller ends up in a drawer as soon as things feel better.** That's exactly backwards. **The controller is the one keeping you out of the hospital, and it only works if you take it on the good days too** — the day you feel fine is the day it's doing its job.

lung-reliever-frequency-warning.label: Reaching for the rescue inhaler more often is a warning
lung-reliever-frequency-warning.say: When the rescue inhaler starts getting used more than it used to, that isn't 'good thing I had it on me' — **it's the signal that the underlying problem isn't controlled.** An easy measure to keep in your head: **needing it more than a couple of times a week, and waking up at night needing it counts, means it's time to have the medicines looked at** — not time to pick up another canister. One more thing worth knowing for asthma: the guidelines changed a few years back, and **a plain albuterol rescue inhaler on its own is no longer considered adequate treatment** — something that settles the inflammation has to be in there too. If albuterol is the only inhaler you own, bring exactly that up at your next visit.

lung-inhaler-technique.label: Have somebody watch you take it
lung-inhaler-technique.say: When the technique is off, the medicine coats the inside of your mouth and never reaches the lungs — and **study after study finds most people are making at least one mistake, usually without any idea of it.** The fix is free and quick: **take your inhalers to the pharmacy, or to your next appointment, and ask them to watch you use one.** Pharmacists and respiratory therapists do this every day; it takes two minutes. The usual culprits are not shaking it, pressing and breathing in at slightly different moments, and not holding your breath afterwards. **Ask about a spacer** — the chamber that snaps onto the end makes the timing much more forgiving. And **with any inhaler that has a steroid in it, rinse your mouth and spit afterwards**, or you'll end up with thrush.

lung-dont-stop-controller.label: Feeling better is the medicine working, not permission to stop
lung-dont-stop-controller.say: The maintenance inhaler is the reason things are going well — not proof you've finished with it. **People stop it, coast a few weeks, and then it comes back, and the flare that follows is usually harder to settle than the last one was.** If it's been good for a long stretch and you'd like to be on less, that's a perfectly fair conversation to have. **Just let the doctor step it down with somebody watching, rather than quietly stopping on your own.**

lung-quit-smoking.label: Quitting is the only thing that slows it down
lung-quit-smoking.say: This part isn't comfortable to hear, so I'll say it straight: **for COPD, the inhalers make you feel better, but quitting smoking is the only thing shown to slow how fast lung function drops off.** And it pays back at any age — there's no point where it stops being worth doing. You also don't have to run on willpower, which has the worst odds of any method there is. **Medicare Part B covers up to eight counseling visits a year at no cost to you, Part D covers the prescription quit medicines, and 1-800-QUIT-NOW puts a free coach on the phone — most state lines will mail you patches or gum for nothing.** Ask your doctor to set it up. People who quit with help do it far more often than people who tough it out alone.

lung-exacerbation-three-signs.label: More phlegm, darker phlegm, more breathless — two out of three
lung-exacerbation-three-signs.say: Three changes belong together: **more phlegm than usual, phlegm turning yellow or green, and being more short of breath than your own normal.** Any two of those and a flare-up is most likely starting — being seen a few days early is far easier than being seen from a hospital bed. **Ask your doctor for a written action plan** so you already know what to do and when to call; plenty of people with COPD have one taped inside a cabinet door. And older folks tend to shrug and say they're fine — **if you're the family member and the phlegm doesn't look right, you're allowed to be the one who says something.**

lung-breathing-and-moving.label: The less you move, the more breathless you get
lung-breathing-and-moving.say: Being short of breath makes people stop moving, then the muscles weaken, then a few steps leave you more breathless than before. **That spiral wears people down worse than the disease itself does.** Walking slowly and stopping when you need to still counts — most days matters far more than distance. **When the breath gets tight, try pursed-lip breathing: in through the nose for a count, then out slowly through pursed lips like you're blowing out a candle, about twice as long as you took in.** Making the out-breath longer settles the panic for a lot of people. And ask about **pulmonary rehab — Medicare Part B covers it for moderate to severe COPD with your doctor's referral.** The people who feel too breathless to exercise are exactly who it was built for.

lung-air-triggers.label: Know your own few triggers
lung-air-triggers.say: Everybody's list is a little different, but the usual suspects are short: **a sudden lungful of cold air, cooking smoke and frying, secondhand smoke, wood stoves and fireplaces, wildfire smoke, strong fragrances and cleaning sprays, and fresh paint or renovation dust.** Working out which two or three actually get you is more useful than trying to guard against everything at once. **Check the air quality before you head out** — the weather app carries it — and on the bad days simply move the walk indoors. A mall or a big store works fine, and plenty of people do exactly that.

lung-vaccines.label: For lungs like yours, the shots pay off more
lung-vaccines.say: When the lungs are already compromised, a bout of flu or pneumonia is often the thing that turns into a hospital stay. **On Medicare, the flu shot, the pneumonia shots and COVID are covered under Part B with no cost-sharing, and RSV runs through your Part D plan at $0 as long as you stay in network.** Your regular pharmacy can look up what you're due for — **tell them you have COPD or asthma**, because that changes what's recommended for you and when.

lung-comfort-remedies.label: Honey, steam and cough drops — where they fit
lung-comfort-remedies.say: Honey in hot tea, a steamy shower, a humidifier, menthol rub, cough drops — **they do genuinely make a raw throat feel better, and there's nothing wrong with the comfort of them.** Just keep the line clear: **not one of them opens an airway that has tightened up.** So use them if they help, but never in place of the inhaler, and **don't let feeling a bit better be the reason the medicine gets put off** — that's how a rough night turns into an emergency room. Strong menthol and essential oils set some people's airways off, so if you cough more afterwards, that's your answer about those.

lung-refer.label: The ones that can't wait
lung-refer.say: **Call 911 right now for any of these: only getting a few words out before you have to stop and breathe, lips or fingernails turning blue or gray, breathless while sitting completely still, or using the rescue inhaler and it isn't helping.** Confusion or unusual sleepiness while working hard to breathe is the same call. **And a fever along with more, thicker phlegm needs to be seen that same day** — don't push it to tomorrow and hope.

stroke-fast-recognize.label: Know the signs, and write down the time
stroke-fast-recognize.say: Having had one stroke makes another more likely, so the whole household should know what it looks like. Hospitals here teach **BE-FAST: Balance suddenly off, Eyes — vision lost or doubled, Face drooping on one side, Arm that can't stay up, Speech slurred or jumbled, and Time.** Time is the part people get wrong. **Note the time they were last known to be normal, then call 911** — and say that time out loud when help arrives. Whether the clot-busting medicine or the procedure to pull the clot out is still on the table hangs entirely on that clock. **Call the ambulance instead of driving them in yourself**: the crew starts working in the driveway and calls ahead so the hospital is ready when you get there.

stroke-dont-stop-antiplatelet.label: Never stop the blood thinner on your own
stroke-dont-stop-antiplatelet.say: The aspirin, Plavix or blood thinner you came home with is there to stop the next one, and for most people it's long-term. **Stopping it on your own — because it bothers your stomach, because you bruise, or because you feel completely fine now — measurably raises the odds of another stroke.** If it's causing you trouble, say so and let the doctor change it rather than quitting quietly. **And before a tooth extraction, any surgery, a colonoscopy or an endoscopy, tell that dentist or that doctor you're on it.** Whether to hold it, and for how many days, is their call — not something you should ever have to work out yourself. Bruising more easily is expected; **black or tarry stools, blood in the urine, or a bad headache after a fall need a call the same day.**

stroke-three-highs-are-the-cause.label: Blood pressure, sugar and cholesterol do the heavy lifting
stroke-three-highs-are-the-cause.say: The medicine blocks part of the risk. The rest of it sits with blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol. **Keeping those three in line is the best-proven way there is to stop a second stroke — better than anything sold in a bottle.** And the single most useful small thing: **take your blood pressure at home, write the numbers down, and hand the list over at the appointment.** One reading in the office tells the doctor much less than two weeks of your own.

stroke-rehab-window.label: The first six months are fastest — and it doesn't stop there
stroke-rehab-window.say: Progress usually comes quickest in the first six months, so that stretch is worth pushing on. **But it isn't a door that shuts.** What actually happens is that people stop, and what they gained slides backwards. The gains that stick come from folding rehab into ordinary life: **reaching for your own cup, doing your own buttons, walking to the bathroom with a hand nearby.** That adds up to more than the hour in the therapy room does. **And if you're ever told the therapy is ending because you've 'plateaued,' know this: Medicare covers skilled therapy to keep function or slow decline. You do not have to be improving to qualify** — lack of improvement, on its own, isn't a valid reason to be cut off. Ask for a re-evaluation.

stroke-swallow-and-pneumonia.label: Coughing at meals is worth acting on
stroke-swallow-and-pneumonia.say: **The complication that most often turns serious after a stroke is pneumonia from food or drink going down the wrong way** — and it usually starts as nothing more than a small cough at meals. Don't file that under normal. Sitting fully upright, small bites, no talking with food in the mouth, and **staying upright for half an hour after eating** all help right away. If it keeps happening, **ask for a swallow evaluation — a speech-language pathologist does it**, and they'll work out the right texture of food and thickness of liquid. Thin liquids like plain water are often the hardest of all, which surprises most families.

stroke-depression-is-part-of-it.label: Low mood afterwards is part of the injury
