stroke-depression-is-part-of-it.say: Feeling low after a stroke is very common — **around a third of survivors** — and it isn't weakness or a change in someone's character. **The injury to the brain itself brings it on**, and it feeds a loop: the person doesn't feel like doing rehab, so recovery slows, so they feel worse. **It's treatable, and treating it tends to help the recovery along too.** Say it out loud at the next appointment; doctors are supposed to be screening for this and often don't get to it. And if you're the family member — you don't have to talk anybody out of it. Sitting and listening does more good than cheering up does.

stroke-caregiver-support.label: You're allowed to hand it over for a while
stroke-caregiver-support.say: Caring for someone after a stroke isn't hard on any one day — it's hard because there's no end in sight. **Call the Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116 (weekdays, not around the clock) and they'll connect you to your Area Agency on Aging.** That's the door to respite care — somebody covering so you can sleep or take a few days — plus adult day programs, home health aides, equipment, and caregiver support groups. **If money is tight, ask specifically about your state's Medicaid home and community-based programs; most states now have a self-directed option, and in many of them a family member can be paid for the hours.** And you don't have to be at breaking point to qualify. This is meant to be used before you get there.

stroke-fall-and-home.label: One weak side means the house has to change
stroke-fall-and-home.say: When one side is weaker, falls are far likelier — and **one broken hip can undo months of rehab in an afternoon.** The list is short: **grab bars in the bathroom, a non-slip mat in the tub, a night light between the bed and the toilet, cords out of the walkway, and the throw rugs gone** — those are the worst offender in the house. One honest note about money: **Original Medicare doesn't pay for grab bars or bathroom modifications.** Some Medicare Advantage plans do, state Medicaid programs often do, and your Area Agency on Aging may run a home-repair program worth asking about. **What Medicare does cover is an occupational therapist walking the house with you** when home health has been ordered — ask for that while it's available.

stroke-blocked-remedies.label: Chelation drips, ginkgo and 'circulation' remedies
stroke-blocked-remedies.say: People get offered chelation drips, IV 'circulation' or vitamin infusions, ginkgo, nattokinase — all sold as clearing out the blood vessels. **Honestly: none of it has evidence behind it as a substitute for the medicine you're on, and the FDA has never approved any over-the-counter chelation product — the harms on record for those include kidney failure and death.** There's a second problem that matters more in your case specifically: **ginkgo, nattokinase and high-dose fish oil all nudge bleeding risk upward, and stacked on top of a blood thinner that is not a small thing.** If you want to try something anyway, **take the actual bottle to your doctor first** and let them read the label.

stroke-refer.label: Call 911, and note the time
stroke-refer.say: **Face drooping, an arm that won't stay up, speech slurred or not making sense — call 911 immediately, and write down the time it started.** These belong on the same list: **sudden loss of vision in one eye or seeing double, sudden violent dizziness where you can't stand up, or the worst headache of your life.** Don't wait to see if it passes, and don't drive yourself. **And a stroke that clears up on its own in a few minutes still needs the emergency room that same day** — a warning stroke is often followed by the real one within days, and that's the one chance to head it off. Far better to go and be told it was nothing.

diar-rehydrate.label: Fluids first — and not by chugging plain water
diar-rehydrate.say: What actually gets people into trouble with diarrhea isn't the diarrhea — it's losing salt along with the water. So start there. Pick up an **oral rehydration solution** at the pharmacy (the pharmacist will know exactly what you mean). Sip it — about 1 to 2 ounces every 5 to 10 minutes. Gulping a whole glass sends you right back to the bathroom. The common mistake is reaching for a sports drink: **too much sugar, too little salt, and the extra sugar pulls more water into the gut** — you end up worse. If a sports drink is truly all you have, cut it half-and-half with water.

diar-eat.label: You don't have to starve — how to eat today
diar-eat.say: The old advice was to stop eating. That's changed — if you can eat, eat. Getting food back in helps the gut lining repair. Go gentle: rice, plain toast, noodles, boiled potatoes, bananas, crackers. Small amounts, five or six times a day rather than three big meals. For a few days, skip milk and dairy, greasy food, sweets and sugary drinks, coffee, and alcohol. And an honest note: the old **BRAT diet — bananas, rice, applesauce, toast — hasn't been shown to beat ordinary bland eating**, and it's short on nutrition. Don't feel you have to stick to it.

diar-milk-pause.label: Why milk needs a few days off (nothing has changed about you)
diar-milk-pause.say: If milk sets you off again after a bout of diarrhea, you haven't suddenly become allergic. The lining of the gut that digests lactose gets stripped, and it takes one to two weeks to grow back. Take a few days to two weeks off, then try half a cup with food. Yogurt and hard cheese are usually tolerated sooner. If someone relies on a nutrition shake for calories, don't just stop it — switch to a lactose-free formula. The pharmacy can point you to one.

diar-dehydration-signs.label: How to tell if they're dehydrated — thirst isn't reliable in older adults
diar-dehydration-signs.say: Older adults lose the thirst signal, so "I'm not thirsty" tells you nothing. Check four concrete things. **Urine** — half a day with none, or dark like strong tea. **Mouth** — look at the tongue, not the lips. **Standing up** — any lightheadedness or graying out. **Skin** — pinch the back of the hand and let go; it should snap back, not settle slowly. Two or more of those and you push fluids harder. If nothing stays down all day, stop managing it at home.

diar-handwash.label: Don't pass it around — hand sanitizer doesn't do much against this one
diar-handwash.say: The winter stomach bug is the one **alcohol hand sanitizer does not reliably kill**. It has to be soap and running water, 20 seconds, between the fingers and under the nails. Before cooking, before helping someone eat, after every bathroom trip. If vomit or stool gets on a floor or toilet, clean it with a diluted bleach solution — about a third of a cup of household bleach in a gallon of water — then wipe with plain water. Gloves and a mask; the fine spray from vomit spreads it too. Separate towels and dishes for a few days. And here's what most people miss: **the virus keeps shedding in stool for a week or two after you feel fine**, so keep washing.

diar-after-antibiotic.label: Diarrhea that started after antibiotics — say this out loud at the visit
diar-after-antibiotic.say: If this started after a course of antibiotics, or after a hospital stay, treat it as its own thing. Antibiotics wipe out the good bacteria and let a stubborn one take over — frequent, foul-smelling stools, sometimes with fever and cramping. **Don't reach for an anti-diarrheal to shut it down**; holding it in makes that one worse. At the visit, volunteer two facts: which antibiotic, and when. That one sentence changes the whole workup.

diar-probiotics.label: Do probiotics help? (Starting with where the money is wasted)
diar-probiotics.dailyCap: Follow the label, usually one dose a day — but not worth buying to stop a routine stomach bug
diar-probiotics.say: I'll give you the straight answer, which may not match what's on the shelf. For ordinary acute gastroenteritis, **two large trials — each with close to a thousand people — found no difference at all between probiotics and placebo**: not in how long the diarrhea lasted, not in vomiting, not in severity. Buying a bottle to stop this episode is money down the drain; spend it on oral rehydration solution instead. One exception: diarrhea **caused by antibiotics** is a different situation, and the evidence there holds up better — worth asking your doctor or pharmacist about. Space it two hours from the antibiotic. And skip it entirely without medical advice if you're immunocompromised, on chemotherapy, or post-transplant — these are live organisms.

diar-antidiarrheal.label: Should you take something to stop it? I won't decide that — but four things are yours today
diar-antidiarrheal.say: Whether to take an anti-diarrheal, and which one, isn't mine to decide — get it wrong and you trap something that needs to come out. But there's one line even a pharmacist will draw flatly: **if there's blood in the stool, if stools are black, or if there's a high fever, don't take one.** For the rest, the pharmacy counter is the fastest answer — tell them three things: how many days, any fever, any blood. Meanwhile, these four need no one's permission: sip oral rehydration solution, eat bland food if you can, park the dairy for a few days, and wash hands with soap for 20 seconds. Most cases settle in two or three days on exactly that.

diar-long-term.label: Still going after two or three weeks? That's a different conversation
diar-long-term.say: Acute diarrhea usually settles in two or three days, a week at the outside. Two or three weeks — or a pattern that's come and gone for months — isn't a stomach bug anymore, so stop treating it like one. Before the GI visit, do one genuinely useful thing: keep two weeks of notes — which days, how many times, what you ate, any cramping, what the stool looked like. That one page saves several rounds of back-and-forth. If weight is dropping too, or there's blood, don't wait on the notes — make the appointment.

diar-refer.label: These don't wait it out at home
diar-refer.say: Go in now for any of these. Blood in the stool, or stools turned black and tarry. Nothing staying down all day, or no urine for half a day or more. High fever, severe abdominal pain, or pain that has settled into the right lower belly. Confusion, hard to rouse, or nearly passing out on standing. If they can walk, urgent care or the ER; if they're barely responsive, **call 911**. Tell the team four things: how many days, roughly how many times a day, the color of the stool and whether there's blood, and any recent antibiotics or hospital stay. Older adults, people with diabetes or on dialysis, and anyone just out of surgery should go in sooner — the same symptoms turn serious faster.

numb-sudden-red-flag.label: First split: did it come on suddenly, or creep up on you?
numb-sudden-red-flag.say: The first thing to sort out isn't where it's numb — it's **how fast it got that way**. **Sudden**, and on one whole side of the body (an arm and the leg on the same side), or with a drooping face, slurred speech, or vision lost in one eye — that isn't a pinched nerve, that's a stroke. **Call 911**, don't wait to see if it passes. The other pattern — creeping on over months, both hands, or always the same fingers — is usually nerve compression or a metabolic cause, and there's time to work it out properly. Those two get handled completely differently, so start there.

numb-carpal-night.label: Wakes you at night, shaking the hand helps — two things you can do tonight
numb-carpal-night.say: Numbness in the thumb, index and middle finger that wakes you at night and eases when you shake the hand out is the classic pattern for a pinched nerve at the wrist. Two things tonight. First, a **night wrist splint** from the pharmacy — the thing that matters is that it holds the wrist **straight**, not bent. Pressure inside that tunnel is lowest with a neutral wrist, and people curl the wrist under themselves in their sleep without knowing. Worn nightly for four to six weeks, most mild-to-moderate cases improve noticeably. Second, daytime habits: don't work or scroll with the wrist hanging down, press a cloth out instead of wringing it, and every half hour shake the hands out and stretch the wrist each way for 10 seconds. If six weeks of splinting changes nothing, or the muscle pad at the base of the thumb is shrinking, or you're dropping things — stop self-managing and get nerve testing.

numb-neck.label: When it's coming from the neck — pillow and posture
numb-neck.say: If the numbness runs from neck or shoulder down the arm into the fingers, and turning or tipping the head makes it worse, the nerve root at the neck is likely the culprit. Take the load off it. **Pillow height first**: lying on your back, the neck shouldn't be arched into a gap or propped so the chin is on the chest; on your side, the pillow should fill the gap from shoulder to ear. Hold the phone up at eye level instead of looking down. Screen top edge roughly at eye height. Every half hour, tuck the chin straight back (make a double chin), hold 5 seconds, 10 times — that resets the head over the neck. **Sleeping on your stomach is the worst of it** — the neck stays twisted all night. Start there. Two or three weeks with no change, see physical therapy.

numb-diabetes.label: With diabetes: one thing slows it down, and one thing to do every day
numb-diabetes.say: If the numbness starts in both feet — soles or toes, like wearing a thin sock, worse at night — high blood sugar may have damaged the small nerves. Straight talk: **there's no drug that repairs nerve already damaged. The only thing proven to slow it down is steady glucose control** — so the thing that looks unrelated is actually the treatment. And one thing every single day: **look at the feet**. Soles, between the toes, the heels. Use a mirror on the floor if you can't bend, or ask family. Once sensation dulls, a blister or a rubbing shoe doesn't hurt, and by the time it's noticed it's deep. The rest of the routine: run a hand inside the shoe before putting it on, never barefoot — not even at home, test bath water with your elbow, cut nails straight across.

numb-b12.label: Some people run low on B12 — and that's a blood test away
numb-b12.say: One cause of numbness is low vitamin B12 — worth asking about, because it's testable and correctable. Who runs low: people on **metformin** long-term (roughly one to three in ten have low or low-normal B12), long-time vegans, anyone who's had stomach or weight-loss surgery, and people on long-term acid-reducing medicines. If that's you and you're numb, say one sentence at the next visit: "Could we check my B12 while we're at it?" Most doctors will. One caution — **don't just start high-dose B12 on your own**. If you're not deficient it won't help, and supplementing can mask the clues of another blood problem. Test first, then treat.

numb-posture.label: The pressure kind — gone in a few minutes, nothing to worry about
numb-posture.say: Some numbness genuinely doesn't matter: sleeping on an arm, sitting cross-legged too long, squatting, resting an elbow on a hard table edge during a long phone call. That kind fades within a few minutes, and the pins-and-needles on the way back is the nerve waking up. The test is simple — change position, and if it's clearly better in 5 to 10 minutes it was pressure. If it happens often: don't sleep with an arm under your head or body, don't sit with legs crossed for long stretches, keep elbows off hard edges, and don't take the phone into the bathroom and sit there. What isn't pressure: numbness lasting hours, not helped by moving, or showing up at the same time every day.

numb-alcohol.label: Long-term drinking causes this too — and stopping can turn it around
numb-alcohol.say: Long-term drinking is one of the more common causes of numb hands and feet, and one of the least often said out loud. Alcohol damages the small nerves directly, and it also blocks absorption of several vitamins — the two work together. It usually starts in both feet and works upward. Here's the good news: **this is one of the causes with a real chance of improving** once the drinking stops and nutrition is restored. If the daily amount isn't something willpower can stop, don't try to white-knuckle it — that can be dangerous. Primary care or a behavioral health clinic has both medication and programs. When you raise it with someone, frame it as "this is a cause we can actually do something about," not as an accusation.

numb-nerve-glide.label: Two one-minute moves you can do at home
numb-nerve-glide.say: If it's the compression type, there are two home moves. The evidence is moderate, but the cost is nothing. **Wrist**: arm straight out, palm up; with the other hand gently pull the fingers back until you feel a mild stretch in the forearm; hold 5 seconds, 10 times, two or three rounds a day. **Neck**: chin tucked straight back into a double chin, hold 5 seconds, 10 times. One rule for both: **the numbness must not get worse while you're doing it.** If it does, make the movement smaller. Skip these after surgery, if you've fractured that wrist or your neck, or if a joint is hot and swollen — check with physical therapy first.

numb-blocked.label: "Which kind is it? Do I need surgery?" — I won't judge that, but here's how to ask
numb-blocked.say: Which nerve is pinched, whether you need surgery, whether to be on a nerve medication — I don't judge those. Same numb hand, several possible causes, and it takes an exam and nerve testing to sort out. Guessing over the phone would do you harm. What I can do is get the question asked properly. **Who to see**: neurology or physical medicine for hand numbness alone; orthopedics works too. If you have diabetes, start with the doctor who manages it. **Write these five down and take them in**: which fingers, or the whole hand; when it's worst (night? at work? looking down?); how long, and whether it's getting worse; any weakness or dropping things; your diabetes status and every medication you take. Those five make the visit far faster — and much harder to wave off as "just getting older."

numb-refer.label: These need attention now
numb-refer.say: Don't wait for a clinic appointment for any of these. **Sudden numbness on one whole side**, or with a drooping face, slurred speech, vision lost in one eye, or veering when you walk — **call 911**. **Numbness with progressive weakness** — dropping things, foot dragging, legs giving way. **Both legs numb along with losing bladder or bowel control, or numbness across the groin and inner thighs** — that's spinal cord compression, and a few hours changes the outcome. ER, now. **Numbness that started after an injury** — a fall, a crash, a blow to the neck or back — call 911. At the ER, give them three things: exactly what time it started, where the numbness reaches, and whether there's weakness. The time matters most — some treatments are chosen by the clock.

tin-sudden-red-flag.label: One question first: has hearing dropped in that ear?
tin-sudden-red-flag.say: Most tinnitus builds slowly and isn't urgent — but one kind is, so let me ask this first: is it **one ear**, and has the hearing in that ear dropped over the last few days, or does it feel plugged like being on a plane? If so, that's sudden sensorineural hearing loss, and it's treated as an emergency — ENT today, or the ER if you can't get in. I'm not saying that to scare you; the timing genuinely matters. **People treated within 72 hours recover far more often than people who wait past two weeks.** Please don't give it until next week. If instead it's both ears, has been there for months or years, and hearing hasn't suddenly dropped — no rush. Let's talk about living with it.

tin-not-silence.label: The quieter it gets, the louder it sounds — change this tonight
tin-not-silence.say: A lot of people find it unbearable once they lie down and the room goes quiet. That's not the ear getting worse — there's just nothing else to hear, so it stands out. Tonight's fix is simple: put a little sound in the room. A fan on low, a humidifier, or rain or ocean sound from your phone, or quiet music. The rule is **keep the volume just under the ringing** — noticeable, but not covering it. The point isn't to mask it; it's to stop the ear having only one thing to listen to. Set a 60-minute timer so it isn't running all night. Do it every night for the first week; most people find the third or fourth night much easier. Honestly: this hasn't been shown to beat other approaches in trials. But it costs essentially nothing and you'll notice something the same night.

tin-hearing-aid.label: If hearing has slipped too, a hearing aid is often the biggest single step
tin-hearing-aid.say: A large share of people with tinnitus also have some hearing loss and don't know it. In that case a hearing aid is often what helps most — once the outside world comes back in, the ringing stops being the only thing you can hear. Honest caveat: the strictest evidence reviews say the trials aren't good enough to draw a firm conclusion. But most national guidelines still put it first, and plenty of people get real relief. So the order is: **get a hearing test first** — painless, about 20 minutes. Confirm there's a loss before you buy anything. One useful piece of news: **over-the-counter hearing aids are now sold in the US for mild-to-moderate loss**, without a prescription, and they're a fraction of the old price. Coverage varies a lot by plan — check with yours rather than assuming. I won't guess at benefit rules; a wrong guess costs you a wasted trip.

tin-ginkgo.label: Is ginkgo worth buying? (Plainly: no)
tin-ginkgo.dailyCap: Products are usually 120 to 240 mg a day — but not worth buying for tinnitus
tin-ginkgo.say: Ginkgo is the thing people are pushed toward most for tinnitus, so here's the straight answer. Pooling the trials in people whose main complaint is tinnitus, **ginkgo is close to no different from placebo at three to six months**, and the studies themselves aren't high quality. The money is very likely wasted, and I'd rather you knew. Two groups need extra care: anyone on a blood thinner or anti-platelet medicine — ginkgo stacks onto the bleeding risk — and anyone with a surgery or dental extraction coming up, who should stop at least **14 days ahead**. If you're already taking it and feel it helps, I won't tell you to throw it out. But keep those two things in mind, and don't trade up to a pricier bottle. The same money spent on a hearing test is far better placed.

tin-caffeine-honest.label: You don't have to give up coffee — but some things really do matter
tin-caffeine-honest.say: People are told to quit coffee and tea for tinnitus. Let me save you that. **There's no evidence that cutting caffeine improves tinnitus**, and quitting abruptly can make you feel worse through headache and irritability. If coffee is a pleasure in your day, keep it. (If it's clearly keeping you awake, that's a sleep problem — handled separately.) What actually matters is **loud sound**. Earbuds past halfway, a night of karaoke, fireworks, a leaf blower or power tools — those spike it in the moment and damage hearing over time. Wear plugs; a dollar's worth of foam does the job. And one more: don't keep turning the TV up to hear it better. That's working against yourself.

tin-sleep-stress.label: Stress and poor sleep really do turn up the volume
tin-sleep-stress.say: The ringing itself hasn't changed much — so why are some days so much worse? Attention. When you're tired, wound up, or short on sleep, the brain keeps returning to the sound; the more you notice it, the louder it seems, and the louder it seems the more it grates. So half the work here goes into sleep and mood, not into the ear. Three concrete things: **walk 20 minutes outside every day**, ideally in the morning, sunlight better still — daytime activity and conversation keep attention off the ear; **keep the same bed and wake times**, weekends included, within about an hour; and **no keyed-up TV or phone arguments in the 60 minutes before bed**. One thing worth hearing plainly: **this is not a brain tumor, and it will not make you deaf.** Most tinnitus never turns up a frightening cause. For a lot of people, the thing keeping them awake is the worry, not the sound.

tin-habituation.label: The approach with the best track record is learning not to listen to it
tin-habituation.say: Something plain first, even if it's not what you want to hear: **for most chronic tinnitus, there's no way to make the sound stop.** And yet — most people end up doing well, because it shifts to "I can hear it, and I don't attend to it." That's not a consolation prize; it's the approach with the most consistent evidence behind it. By working on your reaction to it, it moves from a threat sitting next to your ear to background, like the hum of a refrigerator. Clinically it's called cognitive behavioral therapy; ENT or a behavioral health clinician can refer you, and there are self-guided programs built for tinnitus. What the studies show it lowers is **distress**, not volume — I'm not going to blur that. Two mindset shifts that genuinely help: stop checking every day whether it's still there (checking feeds it), and don't spend long stretches alone in a silent room. Most people habituate over a few months to a year or two. It didn't get smaller; it got unimportant.

tin-earwax.label: Sometimes it's just wax — but please don't dig it out yourself
tin-earwax.say: Sometimes the workup finds nothing but impacted wax — especially when the ear also feels full and sounds are muffled, like hearing through a wall. That's the easiest version of this to fix. But don't dig. Cotton swabs push wax deeper, picks scrape the canal or reach the eardrum, and **ear candles don't work and have burned people**. Have it removed at the clinic — suction or an instrument, a few minutes. If it builds up often, ask about softening drops — typically twice a day for three to five days before the appointment, which makes removal much easier. Hearing aid users accumulate wax faster, so a regular check makes a real difference.

tin-meds-blocked.label: "Is it one of my medications?" — I won't judge that, but here's the way to ask
tin-meds-blocked.say: Some medications can cause or worsen tinnitus. Whether **yours** did, I won't judge — the same drug does it to one person and not another, and many are treating conditions you can't go without. **Whatever anyone tells you, do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own.** What you can do is ask well. Photograph or bag up everything you take — prescriptions, over-the-counter, supplements — and say: "The ringing started around [month]. Could any of these be involved?" Then add the most useful clue there is: whether it started after a particular medication changed, and how long after. With that, a pharmacist can narrow it down fast. If one is involved, there's usually an alternative. This isn't a "just live with it" situation.

tin-refer.label: Don't sit on these
tin-refer.say: Stop "waiting to see" for any of these. **One ear only, started in the last few days**, or hearing in that ear has dropped — ENT today; if you can't be seen, go to the ER. **Ringing that pulses in time with your heartbeat**, especially on one side. **Ringing with room-spinning vertigo, unsteadiness, or vomiting.** **Started after a head injury**, or comes with facial numbness, slurred speech, or double vision — that's the ER, and **911 if speech is affected**. On the first one especially: **sudden one-sided hearing loss is a clock problem — starting treatment within 72 hours changes the odds of recovery.** That's the one thing I'd most like you to remember today. At the visit, say three things: when it started, one ear or both, and whether hearing feels worse.
